title: The bee in the closing lotus
hookLine: a bee stays too long inside a lotus, and the petals close at dusk
carry: dama means holding the senses, not hating them

cards: A bee works its way deep into a lotus on a pond, late in the afternoon, drunk on the scent, and stays. And stays. The light goes gold, then gray.

The petals begin to fold inward, slowly, the way lotuses close at evening, and the bee is still inside. The Vivekachudamani puts the bee in a short list of creatures, each one caught by a single sense.
Then it turns to the reader and asks a question.

teach.b: The deer, the elephant, the moth, the fish and the bee: these five die, each bound by one of the five senses, sound, touch, form, taste and smell.

teach.h: WHAT OF ONE CAUGHT BY ALL FIVE?
teach.b: What then of a person, bound by all five? The old explanations fill in each picture. The deer is drawn by a hunter's music.
The elephant by touch. The moth flies into the flame it can't stop looking at. The fish takes the bait for the taste.
And the bee stays in the closing lotus for the smell. Each one is ruined by something good: music, touch, light, food, fragrance. None of them is evil.

The verse doesn't say the senses are wicked. It says a creature pulled by even one of them can lose everything, and asks about someone pulled by all five. You might expect a book about jnana to stay in the head.
This verse brings it down to the body.
Earlier, the book names a discipline it asks of every seeker: dama, restraint of the senses, turning them back from their objects. Not killing them. Holding them.
That's a big reason Hindus fast.

teach.h: HOLD THE SENSES. DON'T HATE THEM.
teach.b: On Ekadashi, or through Navaratri, many skip grains or a meal, not because food is wicked, but to practice holding a sense instead of being held by it. The moth doesn't decide anything. It just flies.
A person can notice the pull before the wings move, and the text treats that small, practical holding as part of the road to the larger knowing.

how: Many Hindus fast on days such as Ekadashi or during Navaratri, often skipping grains or a meal, as practice in restraint of the senses, dama; some students of the Vivekachudamani also memorize short verses like this one and recall them during the day.

a list of the five senses and their organs
giving up all five senses to live in silence

games.q: each creature, one sense — tap the pairs.

s: the verse says the senses are wicked
each creature is ruined by something good: music, touch, light, food, fragrance. the danger is being pulled along.
the verse asks what happens to a person bound by all five senses
after the deer, elephant, moth, fish and bee, it asks: what then of a person bound by all five?
Hindus fast because they believe food is bad
a fast practices dama: holding a sense instead of being held by it. the food was never the problem.

games.q: you're the moth. the flame is bright and warm. what can you do that the moth in the verse doesn't?
o: notice the pull before the wings move.
games.why: the moth just flies. a person can notice which sense has hold of them, and the text treats that noticing as part of the road.

practice: Go through the senses one at a time, slowly, the way the verse lists them: the sound in the room, the weight of the body on the seat, the light behind your eyelids, what's on the tongue, the smell of the air.

Then ask, quietly, which of these pulls at you most, and just see it, without pushing it away. Many Hindus would offer that one up on a fast day, held for God. If you don't pray, choose one hour today to simply hold it, and watch.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani it starts with dama: holding the senses before they carry you off.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: indriya, a sense, the faculty of hearing, touch, sight, taste or smell.

carryVoice: Your line: dama means holding the senses, not hating them. The moth just flies; a person can notice first. See you tomorrow.
